  "text": "When the library stopped stamping return dates, Jean kept the little ink pad in her desk.

The machine printed slips now. Most people left them on the counter.

On Thursday, a man brought back a book about repairing clocks. Between its pages was a photograph of a woman standing beside a motorbike.

“Is this yours?” Jean asked.

He put down his bag.

“I wondered where that had gone.”

She handed it over. The woman wore a scarf tied beneath her chin. One shoe rested on the kerb.

“My sister,” he said. “She never actually rode it.”

Jean smiled.

“She wanted our father to think she did.”

He borrowed the clock book again.

The following Thursday, he told her he had managed to remove the back of the clock.

“Was that difficult?”

“Not especially. Getting it on again might be.”

After that, she set aside books she thought might help. He rejected most of them politely.

In November, he came in without his bag.

“It works,” he said.

“Oh, good.”

“It loses seven minutes a day.”

“That gives you something to do.”

He looked at the returns machine, then at the empty counter.

“My sister used to work here. Years ago.”

“What was her name?”

“Margaret.”

Jean opened her desk drawer. Beneath the ink pad lay an old staff photograph, its corners softened by drawing pins.

They found Margaret in the back row.

“She hated that cardigan,” he said.

Jean turned the photograph over and wrote his name on the back.

“Take it. We have another.”

After he left, she checked the cupboard to see whether they did."
